units.title: Dynamic Idea Unit Segmentation: Entropy-Based Method Adopted
units.summary: The memory system architecture uses an AI-driven dynamic memory management system with LLM Function Calling for memory updates and dynamic idea unit segmentation, moving away from fixed-size chunking. A new segmentation method will be adopted that uses Information Entropy to determine idea unit boundaries. This method dynamically predicts and tests chunks of sentences, adaptively adjusting chunk size based on entropy increase to balance speed and accuracy. This approach dynamically determines idea unit size based on content, connecting related information. An iterative dynamic chunking method, looking both up and down the transcript, is favored over fixed-size methods, with offline processing mitigating time concerns. An evaluation strategy compares this dynamic, entropy-based approach against fixed-size and sentence-by-sentence baselines, analyzing trade-offs. The optimal balance and feasibility of the entropy method, which assesses topic changes with added sentences, remain to be determined, especially given its potential computational cost. The architecture also defines STM and LTM, addresses STM scalability, optimizes retrieval, and outlines a data preparation workflow. A recent finding indicates that using mixed Chinese and English text in memory content does not negatively impact the system's performance.

units.title: Memory Architecture: Selective Forgetting Mechanism Implementation and Retrieval Efficiency
units.summary: The memory architecture redesign continues to address STM-LTM integration, including proposals for a unified tree-like structure and discussions on the role of a forgetting mechanism. A key design consideration for this mechanism is 'selective forgetting,' where the system would need to forget sensitive personal information (e.g., names, phone numbers) while retaining the memory of the event itself. It has been decided to implement this 'selective forgetting' mechanism for the LLM. This mechanism is designed for memory retrieval based on current relevancy during an interaction, with importance updated post-interaction. Re-visiting old topics boosts their importance, and memories with sufficiently high importance will never fade out. A key demonstration of the memory system's value is its ability to 'fade out' old, irrelevant topics, allowing the agent to ignore outdated information and showcase a more intelligent retrieval process compared to standard language models. A key distinction is that LTM is more concise, while STM is more detailed, focusing on retaining information from recent interactions. A counter-argument suggests that a forgetting mechanism might not be necessary to improve retrieval speed, as current semantic and keyword-based search models are already efficient enough, without relying on full LLMs.

units.current_state: The memory architecture redesign continues to address STM-LTM integration, including proposals for a unified tree-like structure and discussions on the role of a forgetting mechanism. A key design consideration for this mechanism is 'selective forgetting,' where the system would need to forget sensitive personal information (e.g., names, phone numbers) while retaining the memory of the event itself. It has been decided to implement this 'selective forgetting' mechanism for the LLM. This mechanism is designed for memory retrieval based on current relevancy during an interaction, with importance updated post-interaction. Re-visiting old topics boosts their importance, and memories with sufficiently high importance will never fade out. A key demonstration of the memory system's value is its ability to 'fade out' old, irrelevant topics, allowing the agent to ignore outdated information and showcase a more intelligent retrieval process compared to standard language models. A key distinction is that LTM is more concise, while STM is more detailed, focusing on retaining information from recent interactions. A counter-argument suggests that a forgetting mechanism might not be necessary to improve retrieval speed, as current semantic and keyword-based search models are already efficient enough, without relying on full LLMs.

units.title: Evaluation Methodology, Experimental Setup, and Dataset Selection for Long-Term Memory Capabilities
units.summary: The project's evaluation methodology is shifting to focus on temporal understanding, proposing new tasks such as tracking abandoned 'dead topics' and identifying final decisions, acknowledging RAG's limitations. A system-level evaluation strategy will be implemented to demonstrate the value of the structured memory system by comparing its overall performance (using its structured STM/LTM) against a standard RAG system that ingests the entire raw transcript. Other evaluation aspects include checking summaries against predefined agendas, implementing safety guardrails, and modeling conversational interruptions. A definitive evaluation plan is pending. For the experimental setup, the BMR series has been selected from the project's dataset. It is proposed to use the team's own meeting dataset for evaluating the memory system's long-term capabilities, as its recent history contains clear examples of method changes and rejected ideas suitable for a demo. An open question also remains regarding whether discussions within the selected BMR series maintain a single, continuous topic or pivot to different subjects. A two-part demo for the May exhibition is planned, which will compare the system's output to a standard RAG model on a historical topic and demonstrate the 'packing' of idea units.

units.current_state: The project's evaluation methodology is shifting to focus on temporal understanding, proposing new tasks such as tracking abandoned 'dead topics' and identifying final decisions, acknowledging RAG's limitations. A system-level evaluation strategy will be implemented to demonstrate the value of the structured memory system by comparing its overall performance (using its structured STM/LTM) against a standard RAG system that ingests the entire raw transcript. Other evaluation aspects include checking summaries against predefined agendas, implementing safety guardrails, and modeling conversational interruptions. A definitive evaluation plan is pending. For the experimental setup, the BMR series has been selected from the project's dataset. It is proposed to use the team's own meeting dataset for evaluating the memory system's long-term capabilities, as its recent history contains clear examples of method changes and rejected ideas suitable for a demo. An open question also remains regarding whether discussions within the selected BMR series maintain a single, continuous topic or pivot to different subjects. A two-part demo for the May exhibition is planned, which will compare the system's output to a standard RAG model on a historical topic and demonstrate the 'packing' of idea units.

units.title: Application Scenario: Mentor Agent Construction and Student Interaction
units.summary: The memory system's application scenario is defined as a 'mentor agent' for student interaction. This agent is constructed from a specific speaker's past conversations and research, allowing users (e.g., students) to interact with an agent that may implicitly carry the original speaker's personality traits. Architectural discussions will focus on the memory system's usage during interaction (retrieval for answering questions), rather than memory store updates.
